title: US nursing-home inspections trigger temporary quality responses while ratings still predict relative mortality
source_unit: US nursing homes, government inspections, facility quality responses, inspection ratings, admissions, and patient mortality

observations.period: Working paper issued July 2025; revised August 2026; US nursing-home inspection and patient evidence

denominator.unit: US nursing homes and patient admissions; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

inspection_response.unit: nursing homes exhibit strong responses to inspections in multiple core dimensions

response_persistence.unit: nearly all inspection responses drop immediately once the inspection is completed

absolute_quality_measurement.unit: inspection ratings are unlikely to reflect absolute nursing-home quality because of strategic responses

relative_quality.unit: inspection ratings predict relative nursing-home quality

patient_mortality.unit: admission to higher-rated nursing homes lowers patient mortality

observations.method: The paper studies government health inspections in the nursing-home sector, measuring facility responses during and after inspections and relating inspection ratings to patient admission and mortality outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose sample counts, effect sizes, the exact mortality window, or the full identification strategy. Strategic responses may affect what ratings measure; the abstract does not establish which specific care inputs drive mortality differences, worker outcomes, prices, or long-run resident wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Nursing-home facilities exposed to inspections and patients admitted to facilities with different inspection ratings.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ratings may partly capture persistent facility differences, patient sorting, market selection, or unobserved care inputs even after the paper’s design; temporary inspection responses can coexist with genuine quality differences, and lower mortality does not identify every dimension of resident experience.

related_sources.claim: California nursing homes manipulate size around a 100-bed staffing threshold, and access is limited particularly for disadvantaged patients.
Nursing-home mergers reduce deficiency citations and direct-care hours, with compliance improvements concentrated in low-severity categories.
Detailed nursing-home financial evidence reports related-party tunneling and a gap between reported and implied investment returns.

boundary: This record adds a measurement and persistence layer to the US nursing-home regulation chain. It does not disclose effect sizes, prove that inspections cause lower mortality, establish absolute quality, or measure worker conditions, resident voice, prices, profits, or long-run access in the same unit.
